title: Design exercise: search autocomplete
summary: A classic design exercise: search-box suggestions within a 100 ms budget at tens of thousands of requests per second. The reference answer precomputes the top ten completions per prefix from an hourly, decayed aggregation of the query log, serves them from in-memory shards by first letters behind a short-TTL edge cache, re-ranks with the user's own recent queries, and treats freshness as a cost dial on the build pipeline.

exercise.prompt: Design the search box suggestions for a large consumer site: as the user types, show the ten most likely completions within the time it takes to type the next character. Suggestions should reflect what people are searching for now, not last year.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Return the top 10 completions for a prefix of 1 to 20 characters; rank by popularity with recency; exclude blocked terms.
Optionally re-rank by the user's own recent queries; update suggestions from the query log within an hour.
100 million searches per day; each search session sends about 5 prefix requests, so 500 million autocomplete requests per day.
Peak 10 times the daily average; a vocabulary of the top 10 million distinct queries worth suggesting.
derive the request rate, the index size and the memory per shard yourself
p99 under 100 ms end to end at the client, which leaves about 20 ms inside the service after network time (assumption).
99.9 percent availability; the box must never block search itself.
Full search, spell correction beyond a fallback, query understanding, ads in suggestions.

clarifying_questions.q: Are suggestions whole queries or next words?
clarifying_questions.a: Whole queries that start with the prefix; mid-word matches are out of scope.
A query trending now should appear within an hour; a query that stopped being popular should fade over days, not vanish at once.
Lightly: the user's own recent queries are boosted among the global candidates; no per-user index.
Case-folded; one language per site locale, each with its own index; typo tolerance only as a fallback when the prefix has no completions.

clarifying_questions.q: Is exactness of popularity counts needed?
clarifying_questions.a: No; approximate counts with hourly refresh are fine.
Blocked terms (a curated list), personal data that appears in queries, and anything seen fewer than a minimum number of times (assumption: 10 in the window).

blocks.text: Two halves. Serving: an edge cache keyed by prefix (the same prefixes repeat constantly, so a short TTL cache absorbs most traffic), an autocomplete service that reads a precomputed top-10 list for the prefix from an in-memory shard and optionally re-ranks it with the user's recent queries. Build: an hourly aggregation of the query log into decayed counts, filtering, and a versioned rebuild of the per-prefix top-10 lists that shards load atomically. The serving side never computes popularity; it only looks up.

blocks.legend: The serving half of the architecture, the same boxes as the neutral diagram's serving frame, one AWS service each: the edge cache is CloudFront, which keeps a response for the max-age its origin sends s7; the load balancer admits only CloudFront s8; the autocomplete service and the prefix shards are ECS on Fargate tasks that call each other by Service Connect names, which balance round robin and remember failures s11; the recent queries and the block list are DynamoDB tables; the fallback suggester is an OpenSearch Service domain with term and phrase suggesters s15, s13. The neutral re-rank box is a code path inside the service task, so it has no box of its own. Two routes keep the neutral rule that a user's list is never shown to anyone else: /suggest has a cache key of the path, the prefix and the locale alone, so the edge shares its answer; a known user's client calls /me/suggest, whose behaviour has caching disabled s50 and whose answer is private, so it always reaches the service; the behaviours for /me/suggest and /blocklist carry an origin request policy that forwards the query string (the prefix and the locale), the Authorization header and, for /blocklist, the cookies of the load balancer's authentication s54, because a cache policy alone decides only what is in the cache key; the service validates the token that the product's sign-in issued (outside this lesson) and learns the user from it, then merges the user's recents with the shared list; the neutral API note says the edge and browser caches share the response, and this section does that for the shared list only. The shard answer is ids, so each service task also loads the query table (id to text, the same file as the score file of the build) when the version pointer moves. Ids are stable across versions (a query keeps its id), so a shard on a newer version and a service still holding the older table agree, and an id the table does not have is dropped from the answer. The block list is changed by operators: the POST goes through a CloudFront behaviour that allows POST s49 and a load balancer rule that authenticates them with Amazon Cognito or an OIDC provider s48; the service writes the table and then calls the CloudFront API to invalidate the term's prefixes s45, a call to its own box because it goes to CloudFront's API and not to the edge. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has moved on. The VPC frames are one VPC in one Region across three Availability Zones.

blocks.legend: The build half of the neutral diagram, one AWS service each: the search service writes each search to an Amazon Data Firehose stream, which delivers objects to S3 under a yyyy/MM/dd/HH prefix s17, s18, and appends it to the user's recents (one item per search, with a TTL of 30 days, mapping the neutral entity's capped list: a read takes the newest 50); EventBridge Scheduler starts one EMR Serverless job every hour; this is a design choice: a universal target may call any API operation that is not read-only s19, and StartJobRun is an EMR Serverless operation s44. The three stages are the neutral aggregator, filter and builder, run as one Spark application s20 that is configured with the VPC's private subnets, so that it can reach the OpenSearch domain s51. The builder writes the shard files and the query table to S3 and the shard tasks pull each new version, which S3's read-after-write consistency makes safe s21; it also bulk-updates the fallback suggester's index in the OpenSearch domain, upserting the queries whose score changed and deleting the blocked ones s52. The decayed scores (the neutral Query entity's score) are the query table, one file per version with the id, the text and the score: the job reads the previous file, decays the old scores (yesterday weighs half, assumption), adds the last hour, and writes the new file with the version; the service tasks read the same file to turn ids into text. When the job moves the pointer it publishes one metric, a published version, and when it refuses a version it publishes a refusal; the age alarm sums the first over 2 hours and treats missing data as breaching s55, so a run that fails, runs out of memory or never starts, and so publishes nothing, fires it as well as a refusal does; CloudWatch is not drawn. The block list and recents tables are the boxes the neutral diagram leaves implicit. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has moved on.

blocks.text: The read path through AWS, part a: the keystroke reaches the edge; a shared request that the edge has seen is answered there, and any other goes through the load balancer to a shard.

blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed. Edge is CloudFront in front of the load balancer, drawn as one lane here and in every sequence diagram below. A /suggest request has a cache key of the prefix and the locale alone, so a hit is answered at the edge for as long as the origin's Cache-Control max-age allows s7; a /me/suggest request always continues, because its behaviour has caching disabled s50. The load balancer sends a request only to a healthy task s10, s9. The shard name is a Service Connect name, whose proxy picks a replica round robin and remembers failures s11; a retry goes to another replica before any reply.

blocks.text: A hit on /suggest never leaves the edge; a /me/suggest request never hits. The service picks the shard group from the first characters of the prefix; if the replica it was given is slow or down, the retry goes to another replica of the same group.
Part b: the ids become text, the user's recents are merged in for /me/suggest, the fallback is asked when the prefix has no entry, and the answer goes back with the cache header that fits it.

blocks.legend: A user's recents are items under the user id, one per search, each with a TTL that DynamoDB deletes within a few days of the expiry time s12, so the service ignores entries older than 30 days when it reads; the newest 50 are what a read takes. The shared list is the same for everyone and is cached; the merged list contains one user's queries and is marked private with no-store, so no shared cache keeps it, which is the neutral rule that a user's queries are never shown to another user. A term or phrase suggester is what OpenSearch offers for corrections s15. If the DynamoDB read is throttled or slow the service answers with the shared list; personalisation is optional. The fallback's answer is text, so the service filters it against its in-memory block list, refreshed every minute, before it returns it; the domain itself is refreshed only by the hourly _bulk, so without that filter a blocked term could come back through it for up to an hour.

blocks.text: The recents are an optional boost: without them, or with a failed read, the shared list is returned. The shared answer carries Cache-Control max-age=60; a merged answer never does.

The build path through AWS: one run an hour, nothing on the request path waits for it; the step numbers run on through the whole section.

blocks.legend: Each task polls the pointer and reads its own file: a shard task its shard file, a service task the query table; because S3 reads after a write always return the new object s21, a task that sees the new pointer finds every file under it, and the pointer is written after the files and after the domain update. A failed or refused job leaves the pointer alone, so the shards keep serving the last good version while the age alarm (over 2 hours) fires: the alarm is on the job's published-version metric and treats missing data as breaching s55, so it fires for a run that fails or never starts, which publishes nothing, as well as for a refusal. The schedule starts the job with a universal target, a design choice: the Scheduler page says universal targets may call API operations of many services and refuses only read-only ones s19, and StartJobRun is an EMR Serverless operation s44; the job releases its capacity when it finishes s20. The query table is read at step 20 and written, with the shard files, at step 24, so a refused version keeps the previous scores. Ids are stable across versions, so a task on a newer version and a task on an older one agree, and an id the query table lacks is dropped from the answer. The _bulk request upserts the queries whose score changed and deletes the blocked terms in the domain's index s52.

blocks.text: The pointer is written last, after every shard file, the query table and the domain update, so a task that reads the new pointer never finds a missing file; the old version stays in the bucket so that an operator can pin it.
The block list path: how a term leaves the suggestions within minutes, without a rebuild.

the operator, the behaviour allows POST Edge->>AS: HTTP, a healthy task AS->>DDB: PutItem, the blocked term DDB-->>AS: ok AS->>CFA: CreateInvalidation, the prefixes Note over AS,CFA: one path per prefix,

blocks.legend: The operator endpoint is part of the service, as in the neutral design: it writes the list and purges the prefix keys itself, with a task role that may call CreateInvalidation on the distribution s45; the call reaches the CloudFront API through the interface endpoint that AWS PrivateLink lists for CloudFront s43, which this lesson assumes carries CreateInvalidation (no page says so; a NAT gateway is the alternative for that one call). The POST is allowed through CloudFront only on this path s49 and is authenticated at the load balancer s48, so no client can change the list. The list takes effect at every task within a minute, at its next Scan, and at the edge when the invalidation completes, without waiting for a build; the next build drops the term from the index. Invalidation removes the cached copies before they expire s24; without it the term lingers for up to the 60 s of the TTL. Invalidation paths are priced beyond a free monthly allowance, and a blocked term has up to 20 prefixes per locale.

blocks.caption: Identity and network: who may call what, over which endpoint, and what is public. The public entries are CloudFront and the load balancer behind it, which sits in public subnets and admits only CloudFront. The ECS services, the shard tasks, the OpenSearch domain and the job run in private subnets across three Availability Zones in awsvpc mode, one network interface per task, each service under its own IAM task role, so permissions go to the task and not to a host. A task in a private subnet pulls its image through the Amazon ECR interface endpoints and an S3 gateway endpoint, and this design uses those, not a NAT gateway. Each service also has a task execution role, separate from its task role, that pulls the image and writes its logs s25.

blocks.caption: The prefix index: in-memory maps in the shard tasks, ElastiCache for Valkey, OpenSearch Service or DynamoDB.

rows.option: In-memory maps in ECS on Fargate shard tasks, loaded from versioned files in S3
rows.pick_when: the structure is rebuilt offline and swapped whole, the lookups are by exact prefix, and the lowest latency and the simplest serving code are wanted
rows.avoid_when: several different services must share one copy of the index, or the index outgrows what a task can hold twice over while a new version loads beside the old one
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The index is rebuilt every hour and swapped as a unit, a lookup is one map read, and a shard task loads the next version beside the current one and then switches pointers.

rows.pick_when: many services or tasks share one copy of the data, a restart must not reload it, and the data is small keys and values, such as a hash of prefix to top-10 list
rows.avoid_when: the whole dataset is replaced every hour: a copy loaded beside the old one doubles the memory you pay for, and the swap needs a version pointer that every client honours
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Replacing every entry each hour and keeping the old version beside it doubles the memory, and the shard tasks already hold the index next to the code that reads it.

rows.pick_when: the same cluster also serves full-text search, filters or analytics, and the completion suggester's in-memory finite-state transducer fits the query shape
rows.avoid_when: a rebuild and swap of precomputed top-10 lists is the whole job, so a cluster of master and data nodes would be paid for to hold a map
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the index, because the lists are precomputed and a map lookup needs no engine; kept for the fallback only, where a term or phrase suggester is the whole job.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB, with DAX in front
rows.pick_when: entries change one at a time, the table must grow without limit, and the reads are plain item lookups
rows.avoid_when: a rebuild rewrites every entry each hour: 100 million item writes an hour is about $45,000 a month in write units at on-demand prices
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Every hourly build would rewrite every prefix entry, at the cost named beside it, for a lookup that a map answers for the price of its memory.

blocks.caption: The hourly build: EMR Serverless, AWS Glue or Amazon Athena.

rows.pick_when: the job is code and not only a query: a decayed score, a filter against a list and a custom index file for every shard, run at set times, with capacity released when the job ends
rows.avoid_when: the whole job is one SQL statement over data already in S3, or a team wants a visual ETL tool and a shared data catalog
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The build is a Spark job of three stages that writes the shard files in the format the shard tasks load, one run an hour, billed by the vCPU-hour and GB-hour it uses while it runs.

rows.pick_when: a team wants visual ETL pipelines and a centralized data catalog that other jobs and queries also read
rows.avoid_when: there is one job and one consumer, so the catalog is machinery without a user
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. One job, one consumer and no shared catalog leave Glue's strength unused; it becomes the move if other teams start to read the query log as a table.

rows.pick_when: the work is ad hoc or scheduled SQL over files in S3 and the result is a table
rows.avoid_when: the output is custom index files and the logic is more than SQL
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the build. A top 10 per prefix over a decayed score can be written as SQL, but the shard files are not a table; Athena suits the analysts' questions about the query log instead.

blocks.caption: The query log: Amazon Data Firehose to S3, Kinesis Data Streams or SQS.

rows.option: Amazon Data Firehose delivering to S3
rows.pick_when: records are archived for a batch to read later, nothing reads them as they arrive, and nobody wants to run shards or a delivery application
rows.avoid_when: consumers must read records as they arrive, replay them, or run several independent readers
rows.example: For this design: chosen. One hourly reader takes the last hour's objects from S3, and the delivery, the batching and the time prefix are Firehose's job; the bill is per GB in 5 KB increments per record.

rows.pick_when: several consumers read the same records in order, or a streaming job needs windows of seconds to minutes, and retained records can be replayed
rows.avoid_when: the only reader is a batch job that reads an hour at a time, so stream capacity is paid for to hold data that S3 would hold
rows.example: For this design: not yet. It is the move when the trending lane arrives: a five-minute streaming count needs a stream to read, and Firehose can still land the same records in S3 for the hourly build.

rows.pick_when: each message is a unit of work that one consumer takes, processes and deletes
rows.avoid_when: the records are an event log read in bulk and not tasks worked one at a time
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A search record is not a task; a hundred million of them a day would be a hundred million messages to receive and delete, for a batch that wants files.

blocks.caption: The autocomplete service and the shard tasks: ECS on Fargate, Lambda or EKS.

rows.pick_when: steady container services, including ones that hold data in memory and load it at start, with no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the load is bursty and mostly idle, or a Kubernetes estate already exists
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the service and the shards, on Arm tasks across three Availability Zones: the service scaled on request rate, each shard group on its own traffic, three replicas per group.

rows.pick_when: short stateless handlers with low or spiky traffic, where paying per request beats paying for idle tasks
rows.avoid_when: a handler needs a large in-memory index: every execution environment would load its own copy at each cold start, and per-request billing at a steady high rate costs more than tasks
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The suggest handler is stateless, but the index is the point of the shards; a function per request would reload the index or call it remotely, and the edge already turns the burst into a steady origin rate.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and needs its ecosystem
rows.avoid_when: the workload is two kinds of container and a small team; the upgrade cadence buys nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Two kinds of task and no Kubernetes estate; a cluster brings three major releases a year to track.

blocks.caption: The recent queries and the block list: DynamoDB or ElastiCache for Valkey.

rows.pick_when: per-user records are read by key, expire by age and must survive a restart, and the reads are moderate because the shared lists come from the edge
rows.avoid_when: every request would read the record at a latency only a memory cache gives, and losing the data would not matter
rows.example: For this design: chosen. A user's recents are items under the user id, one per search, written by the search service with an expiry; the service queries the newest 50 for a known user; the block list is a small table that the same service reads every minute.

rows.option: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, with expiry
rows.pick_when: the per-user data is a cache, it is read on every request, and losing it is fine
rows.avoid_when: the records must survive a node loss because they are what the user typed
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The recents are read only for known users' requests, so DynamoDB's latency is enough, and a cluster bought by the node-hour to hold personal data in memory buys little.

blocks.caption: The design reviewed against the six Well-Architected pillars.
columns: what it asks of this design
rows: make frequent, small, reversible changes; anticipate failure; learn from operational events

a lower hit ratio or more known users multiplies the origin lines; the TTL and the share are tuned from measurement, not guessed
maximize utilization; use managed services; understand your impact
Arm Fargate tasks; EMR Serverless releasing capacity after each job; the edge cache avoiding origin work for the repeated prefixes
three replicas per shard group sit idle at night

blocks.text: The edge requests are about three quarters of the priced total at both sizes; the neutral table shows more than ninety-five percent because this one also prices the origin tasks for known users, the shard tasks, the reads and writes of the recents, the fallback domain and the log ingestion. The levers are the hit ratio of the shared requests and the share of requests from known users, which the edge never keeps. The fallback suggester, a domain of six nodes for a path taken only when a prefix has no entry, costs more at the design point than the shard tasks it backs up.

Sizing assumptions behind the task counts: a service task answers about a thousand requests a second and a shard task about two thousand lookups a second, so the peak of 21,460 requests a second that reaches the service needs 22 service tasks and fits the 12 shard tasks that the index memory already requires.
A service task holds the query table twice while a new version loads: about 0.6 GB at the design point, so tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB serve it.
At ten times the table has a hundred million queries and needs about 6 GB, so the tasks are 1 vCPU and 8 GB; the cell shows what that costs, against $6,344 for tasks of the smaller size.

blocks.text: One keystroke, and one hourly build; the step numbers run on across the three parts.
Part a: the client asks, the edge cache answers a prefix it has seen, and a miss goes to a shard.

blocks.text: The serving path is a cache in front of a memory lookup; it scales by replicas, and its only risk is a cold start after a deploy, which is why shards load the index from a prebuilt file rather than computing it. The real bottleneck is the build: recomputing top-10 for 100 million prefixes every hour is a batch job over the query log, parallel by prefix range, and its runtime bounds freshness.

blocks.text: Hot shards (common first letters) get more replicas than cold ones, assigned from measured traffic per shard rather than evenly; the edge cache already removes most of the skew because popular prefixes are exactly the cached ones. Discord's message search write-up is the reference for the opposite shape, sharding a search index by owning entity and indexing lazily on first use; it does not fit here because autocomplete has one global vocabulary per locale, but the lesson that index layout follows the query pattern does.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: whole-query completions, freshness within an hour, light personalisation, case folding and locales, what must never be suggested. Say the numbers aloud: 58,000 requests per second at peak after debouncing, 100 million prefixes, about 10 GB of index, a 20 ms service budget inside a 100 ms client target.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Query with a decayed score, PrefixEntry with a top-10 list, UserRecent, IndexVersion; the suggest endpoint with public caching headers.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: the serving half (edge cache, service, in-memory shards, re-rank) and the build half (log, aggregator, filter, versioned builder). Name the three index structures and why precomputed lists make the choice unimportant.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the build pipeline (decay, minimum counts, block list, atomic version swap, freshness bound), then serving under skew (sharding by first letters, replicas by traffic, the edge cache removing the hot prefixes, the fallback deadline).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (regional index files, incremental builds, trending lane, abuse controls), and the L3 sentence: the serving path is trivial on purpose; the design is the build pipeline and its freshness-versus-cost dial.
Context and scope: The search product, the existing query log and its retention, the locales served, and the latency complaints or stale suggestions that motivate the work.
Goals and non-goals: Top-10 completions under 100 ms at p99, freshness within an hour, light personalisation; no full search, no spell correction beyond a fallback, no ads.
Design: This answer fills it: the serving path, the index layout, the hourly build with versioned swap, the fallback.
Alternatives considered: Ranking at request time, trie versus sorted sets versus FST suggester, prefix-hash sharding, a per-user index, with the trade-off table.
